title: Why 1746 happened
hook: a governor's minister, grieving his brother, turned on the Sikhs, and the loss that followed is remembered as the small holocaust

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sikh riders struck a departing army and the captives went back to their villages. Your line was captives brought home. Did you help anyone find their way back, even a little? Today, a darker turn. Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

A body is carried into Lahore. The dead man is Jaspat Rai, an official who rode out against a Sikh band and was killed in the fighting. His brother is Lakhpat Rai, a minister at the governor's court. Tradition says that when Lakhpat Rai heard, he took off his turban, threw it down, and swore he would not put it on again until he had wiped the Sikhs out. One man's grief. Soon it had an army behind it. This path has already walked through what happened next, the small holocaust. Today asks a different question. Not what happened, but why. Today: why 1746 happened.
screen: `A BROTHER KILLED.` → `A TURBAN THROWN DOWN.` → `A VOW OF REVENGE.`

segments.voice: Start with the grief, because it was real. Lakhpat Rai lost his brother. Nobody tells this story pretending that didn't hurt. But watch what the grief turned into. Tradition says he didn't stop at the fighters who had been in that clash. Sikhs living quietly in Lahore were rounded up. Tradition says he went further still: he ordered that the Sikh scriptures not be read, and even that the word gur, which means the Guru but is also the Punjabi word for brown sugar, not be spoken in the city. People were told to call the sugar something else. A man's sorrow had grown into a war on a whole people, down to a word in the market. Then the army marched, and the loss that followed is remembered as the Chhota Ghallughara. Now set beside that a word the Sikh scripture puts in its very first line, describing God: nirvair. Without hate, without enmity. And a line of Guru Arjan in the Granth, here in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. That line sits in the same scripture the minister tried to silence. Then look at how the story is kept. The Ardas, the prayer said at the end of gurdwara gatherings, remembers those who gave their lives for the faith. But it remembers them. It doesn't curse anyone. The names of the dead are carried; the hatred isn't. That's the hard lesson tucked inside this terrible year. Grief is not the danger. Grief is what love does when someone is taken. The danger is the moment grief decides someone must pay, and keeps widening the circle of who that someone is. Lakhpat Rai's story shows that moment. The Sikh way of remembering him shows another one: grief without hate.
screen: `GRIEF THAT TURNED TO REVENGE.` · `EVEN A WORD WAS BANNED.` · `NIRVAIR: WITHOUT HATE.` · `REMEMBERED, NOT CURSED.` · then, large: `GRIEF WITHOUT HATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold grief without hate. Settle, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind a loss of your own, or a wrong done to someone you love. Not the worst one. One you can hold for two minutes. Let the sadness be there. Then notice whether there's a second thing riding along with it: a wish that someone would pay. Don't fight it. Just see it, and gently set it a little apart from the grief, the way you'd set down a heavy bag beside you. Keep the love. Loosen the grip on the blame. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

nirvair, without hate. Tradition says a minister's grief for his brother became a vow of revenge against a whole people, even though the opening line of Sikh scripture names God this way. Today's word.
Your line: grief without hate. Today, if something stings, name the hurt out loud to yourself, and refuse to widen the circle of who's to blame. Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember those who died in the eighteenth-century persecutions in the Ardas, the prayer said at the close of gurdwara gatherings, which honors the martyrs without cursing anyone.

fork.setup: you're Lakhpat Rai. your brother has just been killed in a fight with a Sikh band. what do you do?
options: mourn him, and leave it there.
punish only the men who fought him.
swear to wipe out every Sikh.
fork.reveal: tradition says he threw down his turban and vowed to destroy the Sikhs, and his grief widened into a persecution of a whole people.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nirvair, without hate or enmity, a word from the opening line of the Guru Granth Sahib describing God.

trapdoor: what you thought: 1746 was just a battle the Sikhs lost.
what it means: tradition traces it to one man's grief for his brother, which grew into a vow to destroy a whole people.
what a scholar hears: tradition says the revenge reached even language, with the word gur banned, while the Sikh memory of it, in the Ardas, honors the dead without a curse.

notes: The index hook mentions 'thousands died'; per the claims rule no figure is given in the script. Year one (day 288) already gives estimates.
Jaspat Rai killed in a clash with a Sikh band (traditionally near Eminabad); Lakhpat Rai as diwan of the Lahore governor Yahiya Khan; the thrown-down turban and vow: confirm the telling.
The ban on reading Sikh scripture and on the word 'gur' (jaggery, to be called 'rori' instead) is a well-known tradition; confirm and decide whether to name 'rori'.
Paraphrase of Ang 1299 ('na ko bairi nahi bigana, sagal sang ham kau ban aai'): confirm Ang and attribution to Guru Arjan.
Lakhpat Rai's own religion is deliberately not mentioned so the story is not framed against any community; confirm this framing.
The line 'Grief is what love does when someone is taken' is the script's own image, not a Sikh teaching; confirm it reads that way.

Editor pass: cut the stock line 'grief is love with nowhere to go' and the unsourced 'Sikhs remember 1746 every day'; replaced the 'here's what's striking' stock opener (used on day 848); fixed the garbled word-segment line about the first line of scripture.
Audit pass: replaced the sweeping 'Sikhs hold that line up against stories like this one' with a concrete line tying Ang 1299 to the scripture Lakhpat Rai tried to silence.
